channel.title: The Dig — Software stack: compilers and pulse level
channel.description: Papers relevant to operating, benchmarking, integrating and using a semiconductor spin-qubit quantum computer of at least 16 qubits that is co-located with and integrated into an HPC system. Today's arXiv announcement, ranked against the Software stack: compilers and pulse level preset. Today's ranked reading list leads with 2611.22315, a connectivity-aware transpiler that selects routings after coupling-constrained resynthesis and reports 0.62x the two-qubit gates of Qiskit O3 across 55 benchmarks, and 2611.21270, whose Schmidt-time surrogate and QOC-guided search target pulse-level compilation latency under nearest-neighbor XY coupling; both are directly relevant to compiling for a small, sparsely connected spin-qubit QPU. The skim tier then covers 2611.21578 on temporally correlated leakage and cycle-dependent error accumulation for QEC benchmarking and mitigation, 2611.22260 on circuit-level geometry selection for rectangular surface codes under biased noise, 2611.23009 on dual-rail logical-physical boundary compilation with delayed realization binding, 2611.22166 on a common-clock superconducting qubit control scheme, and 2611.21397 on quantitative millikelvin microwave power measurement for cryogenic control-line calibration. No pay dirt today — 2 to read · 1 to skim.

item.title: Circuit compilation in the quspect quantum SDK: selecting routings after coupling-constrained resynthesis
item.description:
Read new method — quspect compiler uses 0.616 times as many two-qubit gates as Qiskit O3 (95% bootstrap interval 0.555–0.679) at 0.592 times the depth across 55 arXiv circuits on five topologies.

Grade 0.575 · 3.5σ above the day's baseline · matched “Qiskit pulse: programming quantum computers through the cloud with pulses” · Xusheng Xu, Runqing Zhang, Hongtao Xue, Jize Han, Jingwei Wen, Ruoyu Zhou, Lei Jin, Xiaoxiao Hu, Gui-Lu Long

Figure

Geometric-mean ratios of two-qubit gate count and circuit depth relative to Qiskit O3 for 275 cases (55 circuits across five coupling topologies). Values below 1.0 indicate smaller gate counts or shallower depth than Qiskit O3.

Asks

How can circuit compilation combine layout routing and synthesis to prevent routed SWAP gates from inflating post-synthesis gate count and depth?

Before

BQSKit level 2 reached 0.853 and tket 0.930 relative to Qiskit O3 two-qubit gate counts.

But

arXiv set aggregate results informed development; loses to Qiskit on random Clifford circuits on 127- and 156-qubit devices; outputs verified numerically to 10−9 tolerance per matrix element.

Tools

coupling-constrained resynthesis · parity-state A* search · merge-aware routing large-neighborhood search · numerical three-qubit block instantiation

Code. https://github.com/QuSpect/quspect

Abstract

quspect is an open-source quantum computing SDK that provides circuit construction, C++ state-vector simulation with adjoint gradients, support for variational and combinatorial-optimization algorithms, Hamiltonian simulation, control-pulse envelopes and backends for several cloud quantum processors. Here we describe and evaluate its circuit compiler. Routing and synthesis interact: inserting a SWAP can change the circuit structure that later optimization exploits. At its highest optimization level, the compiler evaluates a screened set of routing candidates by their cost after coupling-constrained resynthesis. The pipeline combines parity-state A* search for small CNOT-phase regions, heuristic synthesis for larger regions, and numerical three-qubit instantiation with a per-block 10^-9 check. For a fixed phase polynomial, A* certifies the minimum CX count when it reaches a goal within budget. On an evaluation set of 55 circuits from 41 arXiv papers on five topologies, the compiler uses 0.616 times as many two-qubit gates as Qiskit O3 (95% circuit-cluster bootstrap interval 0.555-0.679) at 0.592 times its depth. BQSKit level 2 reaches 0.853 and tket 0.930. On a 17-qubit superconducting processor, the compiled circuits had the fewest CZ gates in all six scenarios of the main run. Ablations assess the contributions within the integrated pipeline.

item.title: SCOPE: A Physical Execution Latency-Guided Quantum Circuit Compilation Framework
item.description:
Read new method — Circuit compilation guided by an operator Schmidt time lower bound reduces QOC critical-path pulse duration by an equally weighted mean of 42.50% across 13 benchmark instances compared to EPOC, yielding a geometric mean speedup of 2.00.

Grade 0.494 · 2.7σ above the day's baseline · matched “Qiskit pulse: programming quantum computers through the cloud with pulses”

Figure

Surrogate and QOC critical-path latency reductions relative to EPOC across 13 benchmark instances, showing all 104 individual SCOPE runs strictly outperforming baseline EPOC.

Asks

How can circuit compilers evaluate the physical control latency of fused unitary target blocks before computationally expensive pulse optimization?

Before

EPOC and PAQOC; EPOC synthesis relies on unitary distance while PAQOC uses average gate latency for width-based block timing estimates.

But

Evaluated on numerical simulation of a 1D nearest-neighbor chain with fixed coupling limits (Ω/(2π)=100MHz, g‾/(2π)=20MHz), zero drift, zero inter-block coupling, and max block size of 3 qubits.

Tools

operator Schmidt decomposition · quantum optimal control · genetic algorithm · critical-path scheduling

Code. https://github.com/huang4210/SCOPE

Abstract

Quantum computing requires compilers to translate algorithms represented in the quantum circuit model into unitary operations supported by physical devices. Limited coherence time makes physical execution latency an important compilation objective. Gate fusion can shorten pulses, but gate count and depth do not capture fused targets' control demands. Evaluating every candidate with quantum optimal control (QOC) would embed pulse optimization in structural search. We present Schmidt-guided Compilation for Optimized Pulse Execution (SCOPE), driven by an operator Schmidt time surrogate. The target's angular distance from product operators measures the required nonlocal change; dividing it by a coupling-limited evolution-rate bound gives a lower bound on exact implementation time. Trace-angle and waveform constraints complete block scores for critical-path evaluation during genetic search. Local QOC determines final pulse durations. Under a numerical nearest-neighbor control model, all 104 results across 13 instances from four application families have shorter QOC critical-path durations than an adapted efficient pulse generation framework with advanced synthesis for quantum circuits (EPOC). Using eight-run instance means, the equally weighted reduction is 42.50%, with a geometric mean speedup of 2.00. In a shared six-qubit quantum Fourier transform (QFT) ablation, time-surrogate guidance reduces mean QOC duration by 22.21% relative to gate-count guidance and 21.01% relative to depth guidance, validating the surrogate's joint use in fitness evaluation and mutation-region selection.

item.title: PRISM: A Logical-Physical Boundary Compiler for Dual-Rail Qubits
item.description:
Skim new method — Keeping alternative physical gate realizations uncommitted until physical routing reaches an executable layout reduces routing SWAPs by 20.4--30.8% and physical circuit depth by 8.8--10.1% across 25 dual-rail workloads.

Grade 0.543 · 3.2σ above the day's baseline · matched “Tackling the Qubit Mapping Problem for NISQ-Era Quantum Devices” · Evan McKinney, Kun Liu, Harshvardhan K. Babla, Robert J. Schoelkopf, Yongshan Ding

Figure

Bar charts showing relative percentage reductions in routing SWAPs (panels a-c) and physical circuit depth (panels e-g) achieved by PRISM over Greedy across 25 benchmarks on grid, hexagonal, and heavy-hex architectures.

Asks

How can quantum compilers resolve the phase-ordering conflict between logical gate expansion into physical circuits and physical routing?

Before

Greedy search that fixes physical gate realizations before routing.

But

Realizations must act on fixed wires without internal SWAPs; unresolved gates sharing a logical qubit remain in program order; SABRE heuristic does not guarantee an optimal route.

Tools

boundary intermediate representation · dual-rail cavity qubits · SABRE physical routing heuristic · simple quotient graph availability mapping

Code. https://github.com/Yale-QCS/prism

Abstract

Quantum computers can encode each logical qubit across multiple physical degrees of freedom so that errors on the physical qubits can be detected or corrected. A compiler must then translate each logical gate into native instructions, and one gate can have several equivalent realizations that interact through different wires. Routing moves those wires, so a realization chosen before routing can force SWAPs that another would avoid, making code expansion and physical routing a phase-ordering problem. PRISM therefore keeps each gate's realizations open across the logical--physical boundary and commits to one only when routing reaches a layout that can execute it. We formalize which physical circuits implement a gate, which respect the fault model, and which the compiler keeps, and define when a gate can execute under a layout. For dual-rail cavity qubits, logical CR_z has four loss-admissible realizations, one per rail pairing, and its logical availability graph is exactly the simple quotient of the occupied device graph by the rail pairs. Across 25 workloads with 7 to 25 logical qubits on three device graphs, PRISM reduces routing SWAPs by 20.4--30.8% and physical depth by 8.8--10.1% relative to a greedy search that fixes each realization before routing. On the grid and hexagonal lattice, the SWAP reductions hold through 32 logical qubits. By shortening routes, PRISM also reduces photon loss on device models and therefore needs 44.3% fewer attempts per retained shot at 16 logical qubits, as a geometric mean over workloads and device graphs, and it lowers decoded logical error in a three-round Steane memory under skip-gate leakage.
